b001: Packaging for a Vietnamese chilli sauce, labelled in Vietnamese and English, with an aggressive brand personality.
b014: A printed reference book on classical cooking technique that should feel definitive.
b016: A deck presenting supply chain data to a food manufacturer's board. It is dense with figures that need to align, and it should read as analytical rather than promotional.
b036: A reservation app for a Japanese kaiseki restaurant, in Japanese and English. It should feel spare and refined, and the Latin must not look coarse beside the Japanese.
b040: A mobile menu for a Tokyo cocktail bar, in Japanese and English. Drinks carry long tasting notes read in very low light, so the type has to stay legible when dimmed, and the whole thing should feel quietly luxurious.
b052: A Russian textbook on food science that should read as precise.
b053: A deck for a Greek food waste campaign presented to industry. Headlines at 52px must feel accusatory and data at 16px must stay precise, so we need tabular figures alongside an extreme heavy weight. Greek tonos must not clip at heading sizes. It is projected in daylit rooms, so contrast matters. Unsparing in tone.
b055: A printed Japanese home cooking book, 250 pages in Japanese and English. Recipes need tabular figures for quantities and times, ingredient lists set at 9pt so legibility at that size is critical, and the Latin must pair with a Japanese Mincho face at matched weight. We want a warm domestic feeling and a true italic for the headnotes.
b058: A printed menu for a nose-to-tail restaurant that should feel unsentimental.
b061: A delivery app for a fried chicken chain built on a loud, aggressive brand. Type must work at 15px for item descriptions and 30px for category headers, needs an extreme heavy weight and a condensed cut for promotional banners, tabular figures for prices, and must stay WCAG AA compliant. It should feel like it is shouting the menu at you.
b062: A mobile app for a Greek fine dining group. Menus set at 16px in Greek and English with long dish descriptions, so it has to stay comfortable, Greek tonos must be correctly placed, and we need a light weight that survives on screen plus true italics for the wine list. Restrained and expensive.
b068: A printed children's cookbook in Russian that should feel fun.
b087: The site for a Japanese convenience store's snack range, in Japanese and English. Product names sit at 20px and nutritional tables at 13px requiring tabular figures. The Latin has to pair with a rounded Japanese face without a weight clash, we need five weights including a very heavy display cut, and WCAG AA compliance throughout. Bright and a bit chaotic.
b104: The website of a Greek olive oil cooperative, written in Greek and English, that should feel established and trustworthy.
b105: A printed collection of Greek family recipes with long personal essays between them, set in Greek. It reads for extended stretches so comfort matters, and it should feel like a family document rather than a publication.
b114: The site for a Vietnamese coffee exporter selling to international buyers, published in Vietnamese and English. It carries origin and grading data that needs to align, and it should read as credible and long established.
b122: Packaging for a Japanese meal replacement product sold internationally. The back panel carries dense nutritional data in Japanese and English that must align, and the brand should read as engineered rather than wholesome.
b130: Packaging for a Russian range of flavoured popcorn. The bag carries product names in Cyrillic at large sizes and ingredients at small ones, and it should feel loud and fun on shelf.
b139: The site for a Russian bubble tea chain aimed at teenagers. Product names at 28px, allergen and ingredient text at 13px requiring real clarity, Cyrillic drawn with genuine personality rather than adapted from the Latin, five weights, and WCAG AA compliance. Bright and slightly absurd.
b188: Packaging for a Vietnamese premium fish sauce sold in export markets. The label carries protein content, origin and ageing data in Vietnamese and English at 7pt inside a fixed area, so a condensed cut with tabular figures is needed and the diacritics must stay distinct at that size. It prints on paper applied to glass. Traditional and authoritative.
b009: A deck for a Russian teachers' union presenting classroom overcrowding data. It should feel confrontational, and the Cyrillic must carry that at headline sizes.
b022: A printed Greek alphabet workbook for young children, set in Greek, that should feel friendly.
b025: A printed Vietnamese secondary school textbook on twentieth century history. Body at 10pt in two columns, heavy use of primary source extracts requiring a distinct italic, Vietnamese diacritics that stay clear at that size on cheap paper, and tabular figures for the chronology tables. The subject is grim and the setting should not soften it. The licence must permit state redistribution.
b031: Packaging for a set of Greek university course readers. The spines carry long Greek titles that must stay legible, and it should feel academic and permanent.
b033: A mobile app for Vietnamese students preparing for high-stakes entrance exams. The tone is deliberately pressuring, and the Vietnamese has to stay legible in dense question text.
b043: A printed anthology of essays used in an undergraduate literature course that should feel refined.
b048: A Japanese online learning platform for mathematics, with the interface in Japanese and English, that should feel precise.
b060: Packaging for a Japanese boxed set of university entrance exam past papers. It carries dense Japanese and English text at small sizes, and it should feel serious and official.
b067: A printed early reading book for six-year-olds. Body at 16pt with generous spacing, single-storey a and g are required because that is what children are taught to write, letterforms must stay unambiguous between b, d, p and q, and we need a bold that does not distort the skeleton. It prints on uncoated stock. Warm and unintimidating.
b074: A mobile app for a university's official student records that should feel institutional.
b088: A Greek university's site for its physics department, written in Greek and English, that should feel precise.
b092: A printed Vietnamese activity book for primary schoolchildren, set in Vietnamese. Text appears at large sizes alongside illustrations, and it should feel energetic while the Vietnamese diacritics stay clear for early readers.
b093: A mobile app helping Greek adults return to education. Users may not have studied in decades, so body sits at 17px minimum with WCAG AA contrast, Greek tonos must be correctly placed, and we need four weights for clear hierarchy. Course codes need unambiguous digits. Encouraging rather than institutional.
b100: A deck for a Japanese kindergarten introducing itself to parents, presented in Japanese with some English, that should feel warm.
b109: A deck presenting a Japanese art university's programmes to international applicants, in Japanese and English. Headlines at 48px, body at 18px, projected and distributed as a PDF. The Latin must pair with a Japanese Mincho face at matched weight and x-height, and we need a light weight that holds when projected plus true italics. Refined and confident.
b133: Packaging for a Russian science kit for children. The box carries experiment instructions at 9pt in Cyrillic that must stay clear on recycled board, safety warnings requiring a heavy weight, and a display cut with personality for the product name. Five weights, and the licence must permit commercial print. Bright and exciting without undermining the safety text.
b142: The website of a small liberal arts college. It should feel personal rather than corporate, and the prospectus text runs long enough to need comfortable reading.
b145: Packaging for a Russian laboratory equipment set used in schools. The box carries specifications and calibration data at 8pt in Russian and English, so a condensed cut with tabular figures and unambiguous digits is required. It prints on corrugated board. Precise and unornamented.
b182: A printed Greek children's novel for eight to twelve year olds, 200 pages at 12pt. Reading sessions run long so comfort is critical, and the Greek must feel inviting rather than formal. We need a true italic for the diary sections, a display cut for the chapter openers, and letterforms that stay unambiguous for developing readers.
b183: The site for a Russian conservatoire. It should feel cultured and a little austere, and the Cyrillic has to carry that at both display and text sizes.
b198: A Vietnamese university engineering textbook, written in Vietnamese with English terminology, that should read as rigorous.
